title: Mangrove Forests: Trees That Live in the Sea
summary: How mangrove trees survive in salty coastal water, why they matter to sea life and coasts, and how Saudi Arabia is planting them.
poll: Planting mangroves is one of the best ways to protect our coasts.

versions.title: Trees in the Sea
versions.text:
Most trees can not live in the sea. Salt would kill them. But a mangrove can! It is a tree that lives on the coast. Its roots sit in salt water.

You can find mangroves in Saudi Arabia. They grow by the Red Sea. They grow by the Gulf, too.

How does it deal with the salt? Its leaves push the salt out. You can see bits of salt on the leaves.

The mud here has not much air. So some roots stick up out of the mud. They look like small sticks. They help the tree get air.

The seeds are strange. They start to grow on the tree. Then they drop off. Some float a long way. They grow in a new spot.

Mangroves give shelter to lots of life. Small fish hide in the roots. Crabs and shrimp live there. Birds make nests in the tops.

The trees help the coast, too. Their roots hold the mud. They slow down big waves.

But people have cut down lots of mangroves. Now Saudi Arabia plants new ones. It has planted lots and lots of them.

versions.title: Mangroves: Trees That Live in the Sea
versions.text:
Most trees would die if their roots sat in salty seawater. Mangroves, however, are trees that grow along warm coasts, right where the land meets the sea. Twice a day, the tide rises and covers their roots, and then it falls again.

Saudi Arabia has mangrove forests along both the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf. Most of them are grey mangroves, which can handle very salty water.

Mangroves have special ways to deal with salt. The grey mangrove pushes extra salt out through its leaves. On a sunny day, you can see tiny white salt crystals on them.

Mangrove mud contains very little oxygen. To get the air they need, some roots grow upward and poke out of the mud like rows of pencils. These roots take in oxygen when the tide is low.

Mangrove seeds begin to grow while they are still on the tree. When a seedling drops, it may float away on the water and take root on a distant shore.

Mangrove forests are like a nursery for sea life. Young fish, crabs, and shrimp hide among the roots until they are big enough to survive in the open sea. Birds nest in the branches.

The roots also hold mud in place, which prevents erosion, and they slow down strong waves during storms.

People have cut down many mangroves to build houses and farms. To protect them, Saudi Arabia has planted millions of new mangrove seedlings.

versions.title: Mangroves: Forests Between Land and Sea
versions.text:
Most trees would quickly perish if their roots were soaked in salty seawater. Mangroves, however, are remarkable trees that flourish along tropical and subtropical coasts, precisely where the land meets the sea. Twice a day, the tide rises to submerge their roots and then gradually retreats again.

Mangroves grow along the coasts of more than 100 countries, mostly in warm regions near the equator. In Saudi Arabia, some of the best-known stands surround the Farasan Islands in the Red Sea, where they shelter turtles, fish, and migrating birds within a protected marine area.

Saudi Arabia has mangrove forests along both the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf, and most of them consist of grey mangroves, a species that can tolerate extremely salty water.

Every mangrove depends on several clever adaptations, and the grey mangrove releases excess salt through tiny glands in its leaves, so on a sunny day small white salt crystals glisten on their surfaces.

The muddy sediment around mangroves contains very little oxygen. To breathe, some roots grow upward and protrude from the mud like rows of pencils, absorbing oxygen whenever the tide is low.

Mangrove seeds begin to develop while they are still attached to the parent tree. The resulting young plant, called a propagule, eventually drops and may drift on ocean currents before taking root on a distant shore.

Mangrove forests function as a nursery for marine life, because young fish, crabs, and shrimp shelter among the tangled roots until they are large enough to survive in the open sea. Birds also nest in the branches above, making the whole ecosystem rich and productive.

The roots trap sediment and hold it in place, which prevents erosion, and they reduce the force of powerful waves during storms. Mangroves also store large amounts of carbon in their waterlogged mud, often more per hectare than many forests on land, which helps slow climate change.

People have cleared many mangroves to make room for buildings, farms, and roads. To restore these valuable forests, Saudi Arabia has planted millions of mangrove seedlings along its coastline as part of the Saudi Green Initiative.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says planting mangroves is one of the best ways to protect our coasts. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with at least three pieces of evidence from the article.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I used at least three pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how each piece of evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that planting mangroves is one of the best ways to protect our coasts, because the article gives strong evidence for how valuable this ecosystem truly is. First, mangrove roots hold sediment and mud in place, which prevents erosion and keeps the coastline from washing away. Second, mangroves reduce the force of strong waves during storms, directly protecting coastal communities from damage. Third, mangroves function as a nursery for sea life, sheltering young fish, crabs, and shrimp among their roots until the animals are ready for the open sea, which keeps the wider ecosystem healthy. Because mangroves protect the coast physically while also supporting the animals that depend on it, planting more of them is clearly one of the smartest ways to protect our coasts.
